pain_point: Polymer/elastomer blade edge destroyed by hot fused metal
what_happened: A hobbyist 500 W fiber + galvo SLM build (2026): the printed-plastic blade with a silicone-cord edge was damaged by scraping over hot, freshly fused metal; a stainless blade gave 'much more consistent performance'
root_cause: Polymer edge meets just-fused tracks and spatter far above its temperature rating
implication_for_this_design: The FKM/silicone-cord blade option (low-profile.md §3) would run over 200 °C plates plus fresh tracks well above FKM's 204 °C rating; silicone wear debris is also a Si source
design_element: recoater blade cartridge (elastomer options)
recommended_check_or_change: Keep HSS as default; allow elastomer blades only for unheated, curl-prone trial builds; inspect after every build and log blade type in the dataset; prefer a carbon-fibre brush as the compliant option at 200 °C
evidence: secondary news write-up of a hobby build (anecdotal)

pain_point: Rigid spreader jams at a gap smaller than the coarse powder
what_happened: Heriot-Watt open-architecture PBF (Bidare et al. 2017): tungsten-carbide knife edges and cylinders set 50 µm above the plate both 'jammed by the build-up of particles between the rigid spreader and the build plate'; they moved to a 3 mm silicone cord, and the ~10 mm/s spreader then dominated the ~1.5 h build of 5 mm cubes. Skácelík et al. 2026 (via Edison): rigid ceramic blades left collision and rebound marks while compliant rubber imposed little stress even with the gap closed
root_cause: Particles larger than the gap wedge under a rigid, non-compliant edge
implication_for_this_design: Our HSS blade runs 0.05 mm above plate and floor (low-profile.md §4.1) with 15-63 µm powder, so D90 > gap on the first layers, exactly Heriot-Watt's failing case; the stiffened holder (3.4 µm deflection) will not give way
design_element: recoater blade, blade holder, recoater servo
recommended_check_or_change: Set the first-layer gap to >= 2 x D90 (~0.10-0.13 mm) and step it down; log ClearPath torque on every stroke and pause on a spike; fit the dowel + magnet breakaway holder (hot-swap.md §3.3) as a crash fuse; keep a compliant cartridge for curl-prone campaigns

pain_point: Effective powder layer is not the Z step for the first layers
what_happened: Bidare et al. 2017 eq. 1: layer 1 equals the spreader height (50 µm); each later layer adds (z-step - consolidation) and the series converges to z-step / consolidation fraction after several layers
root_cause: Each melted layer shrinks (packing ~50 %), so the next layer fills the shrinkage
implication_for_this_design: With 30 µm steps the steady powder layer is ~60 µm; 15 mm screening coupons have a transient base, and the dose factor (1.8) assumes the steady state
design_element: recipe / Z stage / dose calibration
recommended_check_or_change: Build coupons on a 1-2 mm sacrificial base; record the effective layer thickness (layer-camera height or profilometry) per build; calibrate dose against the steady-state layer, not the Z step

pain_point: Unlocking a chamber that is still inert, and optics on a flexing chamber
what_happened: NIST AMMT (Lane et al. 2016): the optics tower is mechanically decoupled because 'pulling vacuum on the chamber will cause it to deflect'; after a build the gas is pumped out, the chamber backfilled with dry air, and the O2 sign 'will turn green only after the oxygen level reaches above 19.5%'
root_cause: Vacuum deflection moves anything fixed to the chamber; argon left in the chamber is breathed by whoever leans in to clean
implication_for_this_design: Our bridge already stands on its own posts (handled). The unload sequence (modules.md §4) vents and releases the guard lock but does not say with what gas or check O2, and the trace analyzer (0-1000 ppm ranges) cannot read 19.5 %
design_element: guard-lock logic, vent valve, O2 instrumentation
recommended_check_or_change: Vent with dry air or CDA through a slow bleed (it also passivates fresh condensate) and add a percent-range O2 cell as a door-unlock permissive at >= 19.5 %

pain_point: Back-reflected and scattered light overheats scan-path mirrors
what_happened: NIST AMMT (Grantham et al., SPIE 9738, 2016): after 7 min at 60 % of 500 W the fused-silica folding mirror measured 220.2 °C (~275 °C estimated after emissivity correction) and its protected-silver coating failed; the SiC scanner mirrors stayed at 82.7 and 58.7 °C; scatter and back-reflection also heated an anodized Al mount; fixes proposed: a silicon substrate, forced-air cooling of the scanner tower, better baffling
root_cause: Low-conductivity substrates and metal coatings absorb scattered and back-reflected 1 µm light; Al melt pools return a large fraction of it
implication_for_this_design: Bare 6061 plates and Al melt pools near normal incidence at the field centre send the most light back; the galvo mirrors, any fold mirror and their mounts see it
design_element: scan head (L5), beam tube, collimator
recommended_check_or_change: Specify dielectric HR mirrors on high-conductivity substrates (Si or SiC) rated >= 500 W CW, no silver or gold; a thermistor on the scan-head mount with a limit; baffle and air-cool the beam path; check mirror temperatures in commissioning at full power
evidence: peer-reviewed SPIE paper via Edison (pages cited; not opened by us)

pain_point: A from-scratch LPBF takes person-years; O2 dominates quality
what_happened: A trade article on DTU's open-source OpenAM-PBF reports 38 man-years of development; a DTU digital-twin study found chamber O2 had the largest standalone effect on its quality metrics and gas-flow speed the smallest
root_cause: Many coupled subsystems; most effort goes into commissioning, gas purity and safety rather than CAD
implication_for_this_design: Our plan aims for a semester with a go/no-go point (README §5)
design_element: phased plan, go/no-go criteria
recommended_check_or_change: Keep the commercial fallback; commission leak-tightness and O2 (phase 2) before laser and spreading optimisation; reuse OpenAM's safety PLC and interlock design rather than inventing one

pain_point: Machine health drifts unless tested on a schedule
what_happened: Kansas City National Security Campus (Hilton & Gray, SFF 2022): a battery of power, alignment, position, caustic, gas flow at several points including near the windows, elevator accuracy and inerting tests; power, alignment, position and gas flow mattered most; poor focus can lower delivered intensity without showing in a power test
root_cause: Lasers, optics, gas flow and axes drift slowly; screening data spans months
implication_for_this_design: An alloy-screening dataset will misread drift as an alloy effect; the 500 W power head is still unsourced (README §3.2)
design_element: supervisor recipes, metrology kit
recommended_check_or_change: Run a monthly health battery logged with each build: power through the cover slide at 5 field points, focus (burn or camera caustic), position grid, gas velocity at plate and under the window, Z step with a dial indicator, purge-to-100-ppm time

pain_point: Recoater strikes on curled or super-elevated edges
what_happened: One Click Metal MPrint+ (Friedo et al., AALE 2026, via Edison): recoater collisions with spatter elevations, warped overhangs or build-up from poor heat dissipation damaged blades, delaminated parts or ended builds, and were a primary cause of build loss; Xact Metal users call 'recoated bumps and cracking' significant problems (3DPrint.com); UniBw: damaged recoater lips leave stripes that also affect adjacent parts, and AlSi10Mg crash specimens kept strength and hardness but lost elongation at break
root_cause: Residual stress and spatter lift material above the next layer; the blade hits it
implication_for_this_design: A screening machine deliberately runs coupons outside the process window, so balling, spatter and curl are expected; coupons on Ø25-75 plates sit close together, one strike streaks its neighbours, and ductility from a struck build is biased low
design_element: HSS blade, layer camera, coupon layout, dataset
recommended_check_or_change: Flag every layer with a strike (servo-torque spike or layer-camera streak) and carry the flag into the dataset (exclude elongation data from struck builds); orient coupon edges at an angle to the blade and space them >= 3-5 mm; put deliberately off-window parameter sets downstream of the others
evidence: peer-reviewed via Edison + primary abstracts (UniBw) + trade press

pain_point: Notched hard blade causes streaks and build failure
what_happened: Georgia Tech (Massey & Saldaña, SFF 2024): HSS blades with EDM notches; the build failed in the region of the largest notch, with local topography deviations up to 0.46 mm and a bead caught in a notch
root_cause: Spatter and super-elevations notch the hard edge; the notch then leaves a ridge of powder each layer
implication_for_this_design: One HSS blade per alloy, reground (low-profile.md §3); nothing yet inspects the edge
design_element: recoater blade (per-alloy consumable)
recommended_check_or_change: Image the blade edge at park every N layers (layer camera via a mirror or a macro camera); regrind or swap when a notch exceeds the layer thickness; keep two blades per alloy

pain_point: Condensate filter fires
what_happened: EOS: LPBF condensate is 'highly reactive, often pyrophoric, ultrafine'; as reported by Fabbaloo, EOS puts the minimum ignition energy of condensate formed under inert gas below 1 mJ, describes filter fires starting from slow oxidation once air reaches the cake, and recommends frequent cleaning, cooling before cleaning, two-person cleaning and a sand tub
root_cause: Fresh, unoxidised nano-metal meets air during a filter change
implication_for_this_design: Our HEPA housing valves off under argon (handled) but nothing specifies how the cake is passivated before the housing is opened
design_element: HEPA housing, cyclone
recommended_check_or_change: Add a controlled passivation step (slow O2 bleed into the closed housing while a thermocouple on the housing is watched), then open; two-person SOP with sand bucket; earth the housing

pain_point: A loading filter quietly cuts the cross-flow
what_happened: A 2024 Ti-6Al-4V study on filter condition and part properties: filter health depends on material, gas flow and plate density, not just hours; a new filter's life was 2,500 h in that setup; EOS uses build time, Renishaw and 3D Systems use pressure drop
root_cause: As the filter loads, a fixed-speed blower moves less gas; spatter and plume removal fall off
implication_for_this_design: Our ~2 m/s cross-flow depends on blower vs HEPA pressure drop; Al alloys, and Mg-bearing ones most, make a lot of condensate
design_element: HEPA housing, blower, cross-flow nozzle
recommended_check_or_change: Fit a differential-pressure transmitter across the HEPA and a flow sensor in the loop; log both per layer; control the blower to a flow set point; change the element on pressure drop
evidence: search-engine extract of an indexed paper

pain_point: Cover-slide fouling gives focus shifts larger than the Rayleigh range
what_happened: Bonhoff et al. (LiM 2017; cited in low-profile.md and the Edison design review): at 400 W, 0.5 % extra absorption on a fused-silica window modelled a -21.6 mm focus shift; contaminated windows measured -22 to -30 mm and the waist grew from 35 to 53 µm while transmission fell < 1 %; an athermal glass (N-FK51A) modelled only -1.3 mm. Fraunhofer (search extract): transmissivity loss up to 5.66 %, peak-intensity loss up to 56.4 %, transient shifts up to 8.3 mm within 1 s
root_cause: Condensate on the slide absorbs; fused silica's thermo-optic coefficient turns that heat into a strong lens within seconds
implication_for_this_design: Our Rayleigh range is ±3.7 mm; the slide is fused silica (low-profile.md §3 chose it for its low clean absorption, which does not help once it is fouled); the photodiode check looks through the same lid, so camera and photodiode ports fog too
design_element: cover slide + gas knife, layer-camera and photodiode ports
recommended_check_or_change: Keep fused silica for the clean pressure window but trial an athermal (N-FK51A-type) cover slide against fused silica on the phase 1 rig; watch the slide (camera or transmission photodiode) with a coverage limit that forces a change; run the gas knife from before exposure to ~2 s after; purge the camera and photodiode ports
evidence: conference paper (Bonhoff; cited in low-profile.md and via Edison) + Fraunhofer abstracts (search extract)

pain_point: Single-point power checks miss non-uniform window fouling
what_happened: UT Austin / Stratasys Direct (Sassaman et al., SFF 2018, Sinterstation 2500, ZnSe window): ~10 % attenuation in one build; 20-25 % after three builds with a standard window vs 3-5 % with a heated window; attenuation varied by up to 3.5 ± 0.25 % across the window; industry practice was one power reading near the centre
root_cause: Contamination is uneven and changes build to build
implication_for_this_design: Our plates sit at the field centre, where a single reading would be taken; the Ø75 field uses other parts of the slide
design_element: power-check procedure, cover slide
recommended_check_or_change: Map transmission through each used slide at >= 5 points; keep slide ID, age and layers in the dataset; fit a slide-life rule

pain_point: Volatile elements leave the alloy being screened
what_happened: Warwick (Liu & Gibbons, SFF 2023): AlSi10Mg powder with 0.440 wt% Mg gave parts with 0.356 wt% typically and 0.272 wt% at the highest energy density; tensile strength fell once Mg dropped below ~0.306 wt%
root_cause: Preferential evaporation of Mg (and Zn, Li) from the melt pool
implication_for_this_design: A screening machine that reports nominal composition mislabels its alloys; Mg/Zn-rich alloys also foul the slide and load the filter faster
design_element: dataset, cover slide, HEPA
recommended_check_or_change: Measure built-coupon composition (ICP or EDS) for each parameter set and store it with the energy density; expect shorter slide and filter life for Mg/Zn alloys

pain_point: Moist Al powder: hydrogen porosity, and drying has side effects
what_happened: Revanur 2024 (thesis, via Edison): water desorbs from powder, walls, porous insulation and seals after backfill and heating; the laser splits it, giving H2 porosity in Al and O2 pick-up; recommends dry-argon flow during warm-up and a dew-point interlock. Vacuum drying AlSi10Mg 18 h at 70 °C removed ~0.05 % mass (preprint); a 2024 Procedia CIRP comparison found furnace and vacuum drying leave an oxide layer that lowers density, in-process laser drying least
root_cause: Adsorbed water splits into H in the melt; drying in air or at temperature grows oxide
implication_for_this_design: Reservoirs are filled in a glovebox or from an oven, carried, docked for days and swapped at atmosphere; the dew-point sensor is not yet a permissive; the heated plate warms felt and seals after the purge
design_element: reservoir (shutter, lid seal), dew-point sensor, purge recipe
recommended_check_or_change: Log dew point at the start of exposure as a permissive (e.g. <= -40 °C); flow dry argon through the loop while the plate heats, then re-check O2 and dew point; seal reservoirs and store filled ones under argon or desiccant; record drying history per lot

pain_point: Steps in the cylinder wall leak powder and bulge layers
what_happened: Formlabs Fuse 1 owners: at a metal 'thermal break' band ~25 mm below the top of the build chamber, gaps of ~1.6 mm under and ~0.8 mm above it; powder leaked into sinkholes; 2 of 3 chambers aborted at that height (another owner: 3 of 6); support confirmed the thermal break; no replacement part, only a chamber swap
root_cause: A discontinuity in the bore wall that the bed seal crosses every build
implication_for_this_design: Our module is a 316 spigot TIG-welded to a 3 mm-wall tube (modules_low.py); the plate's rim wiper crosses the spigot-to-tube joint every build, and the spigot sits in a hotter or colder Al floor
design_element: build module bore (B1), rim wiper, bore seal
recommended_check_or_change: Hone the bore after welding, as one body; gauge the joint for steps (target <= 10 µm); run the piston through a full bed on the phase 0 rig and weigh what leaks past per 100 layers
evidence: user forum with vendor staff replies (anecdotal)

pain_point: Felt bed seals compact and leak; they are wear parts
what_happened: Formlabs support: powder leaks through build-chamber seals, the print-bed felt seal (voids round the cake edge mean check the felt) and the doser seal; the printer's maintenance screen schedules seal cleaning and replacement. The Edison design review found essentially no peer-reviewed leakage or wear data for LPBF piston seals
root_cause: Felt packs with powder and loses its spring; powder at the sliding interface raises friction
implication_for_this_design: Powder past our aramid-felt/PTFE bore seal or rim wiper lands on the heater stack; the thermal FEA says powder in the gaps raises M50's start power to 226 W, above the 150 W installed
design_element: bore seal, rim wiper, heater stack, gland plate
recommended_check_or_change: Count layers per seal set; vacuum under the piston each campaign through the removable gland plate and weigh what is recovered (this machine can publish the leakage data the literature lacks); keep spare seal sets per alloy
evidence: vendor support article (read); literature gap per Edison

pain_point: Short feed must stop or redo the layer
what_happened: Formlabs Error 112: Fuse Vision aborts the print when too little powder is deposited after a recoat; listed causes include the recoater motor assembly, debris in the hopper/debris catcher, and unsieved powder
root_cause: Bridged or contaminated powder and worn feed mechanics
implication_for_this_design: Our fluted roller meters 0.04-0.33 g per dose and the load cell cannot resolve a dose (modules.md §3), so a bridged reservoir or blocked flute is silent
design_element: metering roller, reservoir, layer camera
recommended_check_or_change: Score coverage on every layer with the layer camera and re-dose and re-spread (or pause) before lasing; sieve every powder before filling; put a debris screen above the roller

pain_point: Powder in the plug of a swappable module
what_happened: Formlabs forum: sintered 'sinterworm' defects during preheat on about every second job; Formlabs staff: in most cases caused by imperfect contact on the build-chamber plug, also laurolactam build-up, bent pins or powder in the plug or receptacle
root_cause: Heater and sensor connections on a module that is plugged in and out near powder
implication_for_this_design: Each build module carries M12 heater and type K plugs that are unplugged at every module swap beside the chamber
design_element: module M12 power and thermocouple plugs
recommended_check_or_change: Keep plugs out of the powder path with caps when unplugged; check pins at each swap; let the supervisor check every TC for open circuit and plausible readings before heating
evidence: user forum with vendor staff reply (anecdotal)

pain_point: Purifiers saturate and need long regenerations
what_happened: University SOP: regenerate when O2 and/or H2O stay above 1 ppm; a glovebox-purifier patent cites 12-24 h per regeneration; rising O2 usually traces to gloves, antechamber or feedthroughs
root_cause: Finite getter and sieve capacity; leaks
implication_for_this_design: A purifier on our argon loop is a 'later option' (README §3.4); its regeneration uses H2 forming gas and condensate would foul it; the lab glovebox that fills reservoirs has the same failure modes
design_element: gas loop (purifier option), glovebox SOP
recommended_check_or_change: If a purifier is added, place it after the HEPA with its own valves, budget 12-24 h regenerations, keep forming gas out of the chamber; log glovebox O2/H2O at each reservoir fill
evidence: university SOP + vendor guide (read in search extract)

pain_point: Zirconia O2 sensors read low when H2 or other combustibles are present
what_happened: Process Sensing Technologies: the hot platinum electrode burns combustibles with the sample's O2, so the reading is low; a glovebox-analyzer vendor lists H2 as unacceptable for its zirconia unit and recommends fuel-cell sensors
root_cause: Catalytic combustion at the sensor consumes O2
implication_for_this_design: Our laser permissive rests on one O2 reading; Al melting with moisture makes H2, and organics (potting, any lubricant) outgas; a low-reading sensor gives a false 'safe to lase'
design_element: O2 analyzer choice (SST zirconia vs Ntron), laser permissive
recommended_check_or_change: Choose the permissive sensor technology deliberately (galvanic/electrochemical trace cell, or two technologies cross-checked); span-check monthly with certified O2-in-Ar gas

pain_point: Virtual leaks and porous parts keep feeding O2 after the purge
what_happened: Normandale: a 1/4 in. blind tapped hole with a screw leaving 1/16 in. at the bottom holds 0.049 in³, i.e. 0.6 Torr·L of air; fixes are vented screws and relief paths behind gaps; Pfeiffer: seals in series (double O-rings) risk virtual leaks
root_cause: Trapped air in blind holes, seal interspaces, gaps and porous materials empties slowly
implication_for_this_design: 0.6 Torr·L released into 6.4 L of argon after the last backfill is ~120 ppm air, ~26 ppm O2 per hole (calc). Ours: blind lid and door screw holes, the double FKM rod gland's interspace, gaps behind the lift-out liners, graphite foil, aramid felt and the HEPA medium
design_element: lid/door screws, rod gland, liners, porous parts
recommended_check_or_change: Keep the vented screws; vent the rod-gland interspace to the chamber or pump it; stand the liners off the walls so the gap is open; accept the chamber on rate-of-rise and O2 drift after the third purge
evidence: educational vacuum reference (read) + vendor guide (search extract)

pain_point: O-rings fall out of vertical or upside-down face grooves
what_happened: Parker: undercut (dovetail/half-dovetail) grooves retain O-rings but are hard to machine with critical tolerances and can over-fill; a seal vendor: in a face groove oriented vertically or upside-down 'the O-ring may fall out', so use retention ribs or press-in-place seals
root_cause: Gravity and door motion pull a stretched cord out of a plain rectangular groove
implication_for_this_design: The drop-down door seal lies in a vertical plane; the lid seal is inverted if it is in the lid; the cover-slide drawer's front-plate O-ring is vertical; a robot closing the door many times will eventually pinch a sagging cord
design_element: FKM door seal, lid seal, drawer O-ring
recommended_check_or_change: Put grooves in the chamber body facing up where possible; use half-dovetail or moulded press-in seals on the door and drawer; add a post-close leak test (pump 30 s, rate-of-rise) to the automated sequence

pain_point: Spliced cord O-rings are weakest at the joint
what_happened: Seal vendors: a bonded splice is the weak point and unsuited to extreme pressure or vacuum; a vacuum supplier recommends continuously moulded rings; vulcanized splices perform better
root_cause: Adhesive joints creep, crack and step
implication_for_this_design: The BOM spliced ~2.3 m of 96515K127 FKM cord with a 9262N11 jig (low-profile.md §5)
design_element: lid, door and window seals
recommended_check_or_change: Buy moulded or vulcanized-spliced FKM rings (AS568 sizes for window and drawer; custom vulcanized for lid and door); if splicing in-house, keep joints off corners and latch points and leak-test them

pain_point: Helium leak checks mislead on elastomer seals
what_happened: Normandale: one KF-16 Viton O-ring on a 1 L chamber raises it from 1e-6 to 1e-3 Torr in 222 min by air permeation alone; long helium probing gives a slowly rising signal from permeation, not the sharp rise of a leak; most O-ring materials pass helium more than air
root_cause: Gas permeates elastomers
implication_for_this_design: Commissioning an FKM-sealed chamber; what matters is O2 ingress at +20 mbar argon
design_element: commissioning and leak-test SOP
recommended_check_or_change: Accept on (a) rate-of-rise from <= 1 mbar with the Pirani and (b) O2 rise over 1 h, static, at +20 mbar argon; if helium is used, short sprays, one joint at a time

pain_point: V-ring packing shaft seals are not vacuum seals
what_happened: A distributor listing for an SKF/Chicago Rawhide V-ring gives dirt exclusion as the application, 10 psi max pressure and a 4.35 psi (0.3 bar) max differential; standard industrial lip seals are designed for about 7 psi
root_cause: Exclusion seals lift or leak under a full atmosphere of differential
implication_for_this_design: The recoater drive shaft and the metering-roller shaft pass the wall through PTFE V-ring packing (9572K33), which sees 1 bar at every purge and +20 mbar while building (README §6a already calls these the weak seals)
design_element: recoater shaft feedthrough, roller shaft seal
recommended_check_or_change: Replace both with magnetic-fluid feedthroughs or magnetically coupled drives through a closed can; until then, leak-test each with the shaft turning

pain_point: Backfill overpressure breaks windows
what_happened: UC Berkeley EH&S (2019): a vacuum chamber vented from a nitrogen cylinder and left unattended over-pressurized and its view window shattered; Jefferson Lab: a regulator set to ~250 psi to backfill a glass system broke it; JLab rule: the source relieving vacuum must not exceed 15 psig in any failure mode; microscopy guidance: <= 1-2 psi when backfilling windowed chambers
root_cause: Cylinder pressure behind a regulator or open valve with no adequate relief
implication_for_this_design: Our window, door (60 N per latch at +50 mbar), cover-slide drawer and 'pressure-equalized' slide are designed around vacuum and +20 mbar; argon arrives through a cylinder regulator/flowmeter and NC solenoids; the 0.5 psi relief must pass the full failure flow
design_element: argon manifold, relief valve, door latches, drawer, window
recommended_check_or_change: Size the relief valve's flow at 34 mbar above the worst-case argon flow (valve stuck open); add a fixed restricting orifice upstream; a hardware pressure switch at ~+40 mbar that drops the argon valves; proof-test it
evidence: university and national-lab lessons learned (read in extracts)

pain_point: Pump-down and venting blow powder out of cylinders and hoppers
what_happened: UT's direct-SLS-of-metals patent: 'to prevent ejection of powder from the feed and part side cylinders during chamber evacuation', the void above the bed and the voids below the powder columns are joined by stainless bellows hose, and the evacuation rate is set by bellows valves at each port
root_cause: Gas trapped under a piston or in a hopper headspace escapes through the powder when the chamber pressure drops, and rushes back when it rises
implication_for_this_design: Our under-piston volume (sealed by the rod gland) can only vent through the felt/PTFE bore seal and the powder bed; each reservoir's headspace vents through its powder and the roller; the overflow jar too. 2-3 purges per build
design_element: build module (under-piston void), reservoirs, overflow jar, pump valve
recommended_check_or_change: Give the under-piston void a filtered vent (sintered 316) to the chamber or pump line; vent reservoir lids through a filter; add a soft-pump needle valve for the first ~100 mbar and a soft vent; photograph a full bed after each purge on the phase 0 rig

pain_point: Powder and condensate reach the scroll pump
what_happened: Edwards sells a KF-25 micron filter trap for nXDS dry scroll pumps (5 µm element, 1 µm option) for the inlet 'to protect from debris' sucked from the chamber, or for the exhaust to trap tip-seal dust
root_cause: Purging a powder-filled chamber pulls fines into the pump line; scroll tip seals wear and shed dust
implication_for_this_design: Every purge cycle pulls chamber gas, fines and condensate into the scroll pump, which is not a place to collect pyrophoric dust
design_element: scroll pump, pump line, KF-25 valve
recommended_check_or_change: Put a 1 µm inlet trap on the pump line, pump from a port away from the bed, treat the trap element like the HEPA (passivate, dispose), duct the exhaust out; log pump-down time per purge as a health metric

pain_point: Back-reflection from Al: instability, trips or damage
what_happened: Vendors: reflections from reflective metals cause unstable operation, shutdowns or laser failure; nLIGHT: 'legacy fiber lasers often employ software isolation which shuts off the laser when back-reflection is detected', whereas it dumps the light in an integrated isolator; isolators are integral to pulsed fiber lasers >= 20 W
root_cause: Specular return from a flat melt pool or bare Al plate couples back into the delivery fiber
implication_for_this_design: Our Ø25-75 plates sit at the centre of a non-telecentric field, where the beam is within a few degrees of normal, and first layers hit bare 6061; IPG has not yet confirmed back-reflection protection (quote open item); a software trip would stop builds mid-layer
design_element: laser (L1), plate position, window and cover-slide tilt
recommended_check_or_change: Get IPG's back-reflection rating and trip behaviour in writing; offset the plate from the optical axis or tilt window and slide 2-3° so their reflections miss the aperture; start each plate with a gentler first layer; log the laser's back-reflection alarms

pain_point: Thermal focal shift in the f-theta at 500 W
what_happened: Stubenvoll et al. (Optics Express 2014) measured f-theta lenses under a 500 W Yb fiber laser and cut the focal shift by 60 % with passive compensation; Jenoptik (euspen 2012): absorption in standard optical glass is too high for high power, and fused-silica f-thetas were tested
root_cause: Absorption in multi-element glass lenses heats them and changes focus over minutes
implication_for_this_design: The model uses the Thorlabs FTH160-1064 envelope, which lists only a pulsed damage threshold
design_element: f-theta lens (L6)
recommended_check_or_change: Specify a fused-silica f-theta rated for >= 500 W CW; measure the caustic cold and after 10 min at power; keep the ±3.7 mm Rayleigh budget for lens shift plus cover-slide shift

pain_point: Galvo drift and calibration
what_happened: SCANLAB SCANcube IV 30: offset drift < 20 µrad/K, gain < 35 ppm/K, 8 h drift < 50 µrad / < 50 ppm after a 30 min warm-up. NIST TN 2099 (Lane et al. 2020, via Edison): AMMT's 'mark and measure' calibration burns a 7 x 7 dot grid (~15 W, 100 ms per dot) on black-anodized Al, scans it at 4800 dpi and targets < 1e-3 mm/mm (< 100 µm over 100 mm)
root_cause: Thermal drift of galvo servos and mounts; field distortion needs measured correction
implication_for_this_design: At f = 160 mm, 20 µrad/K is 3.2 µm/K and 100 µrad is 16 µm; the bridge warms from the plate (42-92 W into the chamber) and the laser; cheap marking heads publish worse or no figures
design_element: galvo head, optics bridge
recommended_check_or_change: Put a 30 min warm-up in the recipe; calibrate with a NIST-style dot grid on anodized Al read on a flatbed scanner; scan 3 fiducials outside the coupons each build and image them with the layer camera; log galvo temperature
evidence: vendor datasheet (extract) + NIST technical note via Edison

pain_point: Eye injuries when a beam is assumed off, and during alignment
what_happened: UC Berkeley EH&S: a researcher put a dielectric mirror into a 1 W CW 852 nm beam believed off and took it in the eye (lessons: presume lasers are on, in-use indicators, camera viewing); an earlier Berkeley injury came from a stray reflection while aligning a Class 4 Nd:YAG, with an open beam path and no reflection survey
root_cause: Unknown beam state; open beam paths during alignment
implication_for_this_design: Our Class 1 enclosure covers normal running; the risk is commissioning and alignment of collimator, galvo and window with covers off, and any guard-open service mode
design_element: guard, emission indicator, service mode, guide laser
recommended_check_or_change: No open-beam work above Class 3R without an LSO-approved SOP; align with the guide laser or < 1 W into a dump; show emission state at the tray front and in the REST status; align with cameras, not by eye

pain_point: Water on Al filter dust: hydrogen deflagrations, two dead
what_happened: Shanghai, 14 Sep 2023, at an LPBF machine maker: during a cartridge dust-collector filter swap an operator sprayed tap water on the filter element; hydrogen from the Al alloy dust ignited; later, moving the collector outdoors, water poured on a smoking filter caused a second deflagration; 2 dead, 2 injured (burns over 90 % and 70 %)
root_cause: Al + water makes heat and H2 in a confined housing; ad hoc response to a smouldering filter
implication_for_this_design: modules.md §4 suggests a wet immersion separator vacuum for Al condensate (wet separators make H2 and need H2 venting and sludge handling); low-profile.md routes chilled water through the tray dock to the laser, although the quoted IPG laser is air-cooled
design_element: cleaning-vacuum choice, tray dock services, HEPA SOP
recommended_check_or_change: No water near powder or the filter: drop the chilled-water line from the dock; pick the cleaning vacuum with EHS under NFPA 484 (if wet, H2-vented and never sealed); dry sand and Class D only at the machine

pain_point: Condensate on chamber walls ignites during vacuum cleaning
what_happened: ARIA 50745, Cebazat, France, 22 Sep 2017: Ti soot on the inner walls of an LPBF machine's lasering area ignited when cleaned with an ATEX vacuum; flames spread to the machine's plastic parts; 54 employees evacuated; machine unusable; the risk analysis had not covered the soot; the stepladder used was not earthed
root_cause: Fresh condensate is pyrophoric; friction and air during cleaning ignite it
implication_for_this_design: After every build our lift-out liners, walls, door, drawer and overflow carry Al condensate; cleaning is by vacuum and IPA wipes (low-profile.md §3)
design_element: lift-out liners, chamber interior, cleaning SOP
recommended_check_or_change: Passivate before cleaning (slow air bleed into the closed chamber while a liner thermocouple is watched, or wipe with mineral oil); clean liners outside on a grounded metal tray; keep plastics out of the chamber (already); earth operator and tools

pain_point: Static ignition in a vacuum cleaner with Al dust
what_happened: ARIA 31934 (metallisation plant): an explosion in an operating industrial vacuum connected to suction while a second, switched-off vacuum was being cleaned; aluminium powder inside; static electricity suspected
root_cause: Charged, ungrounded hoses and housings with Al dust inside
implication_for_this_design: Whatever vacuum cleans our chamber (the $3,190 Class II dry HEPA unit or a wet separator) collects Al fines and condensate
design_element: cleaning vacuum and hoses
recommended_check_or_change: Conductive hose and wand bonded to the unit; check bonding before use; one vacuum per alloy family, emptied after use; never service one vacuum while another runs on the same line

pain_point: The AM fire OSHA cited: no Class D, dust not emptied, shop vac
what_happened: Powderpart, Woburn MA, 5 Nov 2013: explosion and fire, third-degree burns to an employee working alone; OSHA: one willful (no Class D extinguishers) and nine serious items, $64,400; dry dust collector not emptied daily or monthly; an unrated shop vac at the sieving station; no way to disconnect sprinklers; fire department not told of water-reactive Ti/Al powders
root_cause: Housekeeping, ignition-source control and emergency planning missing
implication_for_this_design: Class D is specified (handled); overflow jar and filter emptying intervals, lone work, shop vacs and the fire department's knowledge are not
design_element: SOPs, room, fire plan
recommended_check_or_change: Empty the overflow jar every build; no lone work for cleaning or filter changes; ban shop vacs from the area; tell BYU's fire marshal what is stored; keep a powder inventory log

pain_point: Al dust in a closed barrel took on water and blew its lid
what_happened: US metal-products plant (HIAD event 746): Al dust from an outdoor collector was sealed in barrels stored indoors; one took on water, the lid blew off and the dust cloud exploded in a fireball; sprinklers operated
root_cause: Al + water makes H2 in a closed container
implication_for_this_design: Spent HEPA elements, pump-trap elements, overflow powder and liner scrapings need a storage plan
design_element: spent-filter and condensate storage
recommended_check_or_change: Store spent elements and condensate dry, under sand, in grounded metal cans that vent (not gas-tight), away from water lines; label and dispose promptly

pain_point: Accumulated fine metal dust lofted by a small event
what_happened: CSB, Hoeganaes, Gallatin TN, 2011: two iron-powder flash fires and a hydrogen explosion from a corroded pipe that lofted accumulated dust; 5 killed, 3 injured; equipment not sealed; the company knew the hazard from its own tests
root_cause: Fugitive dust accumulates on elevated surfaces until something disperses it
implication_for_this_design: Our inventory is small, but fugitive Al fines will collect inside the guard, on the tray and on VLM surfaces over months
design_element: guard enclosure, tray, VLM, housekeeping
recommended_check_or_change: Wipe-down per campaign; a visible-dust rule; reservoirs sealed for transport; ask EHS to include the VLM in the dust hazard analysis

pain_point: Explosion in a dust collector travels back through ducts
what_happened: CSB, Hayes Lemmerz, Huntington IN, 2003: fine aluminium ignited in a dust collection system whose hazards were not identified; the pressure wave travelled through ductwork into the building; one worker killed
root_cause: Shared collection ducts link the collector to the work area
implication_for_this_design: Our loop is closed and inert with an isolatable HEPA housing (handled); the risk would come from tying the guard or chamber to a house dust-extraction system
design_element: gas loop, exhaust, room services
recommended_check_or_change: Keep the loop closed; never connect the chamber or guard to shared dust extraction; pump exhaust on its own line with a trap

pain_point: SSRs fail shorted; semiconductors are not over-temperature limits
what_happened: Thermal Devices' SSR catalogue: 'the most prevalent concern' is an SSR failing shorted; Watlow: semiconductor power switching devices are 'not legal for over temperature limit or safety devices'; Omron sells SSRs that detect their own short
root_cause: Thermal or transient damage to the switching junction leaves it on
implication_for_this_design: Our Crydom D1D12/D1D20 switches up to 10.4 A DC; the CN708 limit with a mechanical relay is the right architecture if its relay breaks the heater power path
design_element: heater supply (H2), SSR, CN708 limit
recommended_check_or_change: Wire the CN708 relay (or a contactor it drives) in series with the SSR output for every cartridge of the module; proof-test the limit each campaign; fuse each module; sense heater current to catch a shorted SSR at 'off'

pain_point: A heater or sensor backs out of its hole and nothing notices
what_happened: Hackaday 2018: a desktop 3D printer caught fire after its heater cartridge came loose from the heat block; the stock firmware did not detect heating with no temperature change; Prusa's thermal-runaway check trips when the temperature drops > 15 °C for > 45 s, with a dislodged thermistor a listed cause
root_cause: Cycling walks loose parts out of plain holes; control loops then drive full power
implication_for_this_design: Our cartridges sit in vertical holes from below, and the thermocouples also enter from below, so gravity helps them out; a dropped control TC reads low and the PID goes to full power
design_element: heater block, cartridges, type K thermocouples
recommended_check_or_change: Retain every cartridge and thermocouple mechanically (clamp plate or spring-loaded fittings); add supervisor runaway checks (full output with < X °C/min rise; control-limit disagreement > 15 °C) that open the heater supply

pain_point: Cartridge heaters fail at the lead end and when loose in the hole
what_happened: Watlow names contamination, corrosion, over-temperature and lead-wire failure as the main causes; a loose fit makes a cartridge run much hotter than the part; thermal cycling draws material into the lead end and causes arcing; Tempco reports lead failures where temperature exceeded the insulation rating
root_cause: Poor fit, contamination and lead over-temperature
implication_for_this_design: Our lead ends point down into the piston-head pockets, where powder that passes the rim wiper collects; McMaster's 24 V cartridge has PTFE lead insulation and no rating (modules.md §7)
design_element: heater block cartridge holes and lead pockets
recommended_check_or_change: Ream holes to the vendor's fit; buy cartridges with high-temperature (glass or mica) leads and swaged lead exits; seal the lead pockets against powder; insulation-test the cartridges each campaign

pain_point: Thermal cutoff run too close to its rating
what_happened: Therm-O-Disc MICROTEMP datasheet copies: do not expose TCOs to continuous temperatures above Tf - 25 °C; choose a rating above the normal maximum including overshoot; no published DC ratings for MICROTEMP, and DC interruption is application-sensitive
root_cause: Ageing and nuisance opening near Tf; DC arcs are hard to break
implication_for_this_design: Our 240 °C cutoff sits in a block that runs at 204-221 °C with a 225 °C heat-up cap, above Tf - 25 = 215 °C, so it may open mid-build or drift; its DC breaking capacity at 24 V and ~10 A is unverified (modules.md §7)
design_element: thermal cutoff in the heater block
recommended_check_or_change: Move the cutoff to where normal temperature stays <= Tf - 25 °C but a runaway still reaches it, or choose a higher-Tf device with a DC rating; keep the CN708 limit as the primary over-temperature device

pain_point: Fine powder destroys ball screws and profile guides
what_happened: Kuroda: foreign matter in a ball nut causes fast-progressing abnormal wear and can block ball recirculation, use a bellows or cover; a motion-system guide: bellows suit larger particles, fine particles need robust seals or full enclosure; NSK offers side seals against fine graphite and ceramic powder
root_cause: Abrasive fines (Al with an alumina skin) enter the nut and carriage; dry running speeds wear
implication_for_this_design: The recoater rail, carriage (rubber end seals, grease fitting, 175 °F max), ball screw and nut are inside the chamber on the back wall, in Al fines and condensate, while the design also says no lubricant inside
design_element: recoater axis (M1)
recommended_check_or_change: Move the screw and guide outside the gas envelope (arm through a sealed slot or a magnetic coupling), or enclose them in a housing with a slot seal and argon flowing outward; if they stay inside, use sealed, PFPE-lubricated parts under a bellows and inspect each campaign

pain_point: Interlocks get defeated when they block work
what_happened: NIOSH robot fatalities: easily bypassed interlock barriers; an object placed in a gate relay to defeat an interlock; a MIOSHA case of a door interlock defeated with a rag; an integrator recalls a worker who spent 40 minutes disabling one; 'when a safeguard blocks production, users will look to defeat it'
root_cause: Safeguards that cost time invite bypass
implication_for_this_design: Our guard stays locked while lasing, off atmosphere or with the plate above 50 °C (15-40 min cool-down): a person or robot waiting on that is the classic bypass motive; the Omron D4JL uses a separate mechanical actuator that a spare can defeat
design_element: guard-lock switch, safety relay, robot cell
recommended_check_or_change: Use a coded (RFID, high-coding) guard-locking switch or keep spare actuators locked away; show why the door is locked and when it will open; give the robot other work during cool-down; log every lock and unlock; no bypass except an LSO-approved keyed service mode

pain_point: Cohesive powder arches and ratholes, and vibration packs it
what_happened: TU Berlin's synchrotron LPBF on an Aconity MINI base (Uhlmann et al. 2020, via Edison): fine or cohesive powders bridged and clogged the funnel orifice, so vibration motors were added; the geometry worked for spherical 20-63 µm Ti and Ni only. MIT's spreading testbed (Oropeza et al. 2021): a vibrated hopper dispensed < 22 µm steel, with dose depending on vibration pressure (20-60 psi) and time (0.5-20 s), calibrated empirically. Hopper-design guidance: mass-flow cones need walls steeper than 58-71° from horizontal for 10-25° wall friction; vibration can compact cohesive powder further
root_cause: Fine Al tails (< 20 µm) are cohesive; a narrow slot and shallow walls let arches form
implication_for_this_design: Our wedge hoppers have 35° walls over an 8 mm slot with no agitation (modules.md §3); filled reservoirs ride VLM transits and sit docked for days; the Edison review found no study showing 15-45 µm Al flowing through an 8 mm slot without agitation
design_element: S/M/L reservoirs, metering roller
recommended_check_or_change: Measure each powder's flow (Hausner ratio at least) and test arching on the phase 0 rig after a simulated VLM transit; make the slot width adjustable, steepen the walls (>= 60-65° from horizontal) and add a small vibrator or agitator that runs only while dosing; calibrate dose per alloy and fill level

pain_point: Fine Al powder charges on insulators and in dry gas
what_happened: Via Edison: AlSi10Mg picked up about -2.8 to -5.7 nC/m² after contact with stainless steel, depending on flow rate (2026 thesis); drier conditions keep charge longer and small particles can charge opposite to large ones, segregating sizes (Alchikh-Sulaiman 2020 thesis); Galindo et al. 2024 use tribocharging to grade AM powders. AIChE 2021: humidity changes charging and spreadability of AlSi7Mg; Bristol (arXiv 2025): insulating liners charge powder far more than aluminium walls
root_cause: Insulating contact surfaces and very dry gas
implication_for_this_design: Our powder meets PTFE/PFA scrapers, FKM, PTFE V-rings and tag adhesives in argon at a -40 to -60 °C dew point, over a 200 °C plate
design_element: powder-path insulators, blade holder, reservoir
recommended_check_or_change: Bond every metal part in the powder path to chamber ground (the lab's 0.1 Ω check); use dissipative grades where a polymer must touch powder; test spreading on the phase 0 rig in dry argon, not room air
evidence: peer-reviewed and theses via Edison + conference abstract + preprint

pain_point: Pressure forces swamp a load cell across a sealed joint
what_happened: OMEGA: when a hopper is sealed to an independently supported hood by a boot, pressure changes cause weighing error, and venting is required; HBM: the effect equals pressure times the sealed cross-section; OMEGA: total vertical force from connections should stay below 30 x system accuracy x live load
root_cause: A pressure difference acting on the area inside a seal that crosses the weighed load path
implication_for_this_design: Our reservoir rides dock rails on a 2-3 kg single-point cell while its outlet seals to the fixed metering base; a ~20 x 100 mm sealed outlet sees ~4 N (0.4 kg) at +20 mbar and ~200 N at full vacuum, far past the cell's overload (calc)
design_element: reservoir load cell, dock seal
recommended_check_or_change: Keep the pressure boundary out of the load path (seal inside the weighed body or weigh outside the envelope); add overload stops; weigh only at a known chamber pressure with a pressure term; re-tare after each purge
evidence: vendor application notes (read in extract); force is our calc

pain_point: Argon pools out of sight and asphyxiates
what_happened: CSB summary, 30 Jan 2023: argon leaked from an autoclave's seals into a ~4,500 ft³ basement with its ventilation off; two workers who entered died; no forced ventilation or continuous O2 monitoring; LBNL: O2 at the floor can be below 15 % while above 20 % at breathing height
root_cause: Dense inert gas accumulates in low, enclosed spaces
implication_for_this_design: The machine lives on a VLM tray inside an enclosed tower; argon from a leak, the relief valve or the pump exhaust can collect there, and the room O2 monitor is outside it; each build dumps 2-3 chamber volumes plus the loop
design_element: argon via the tray dock, relief-valve outlet, pump exhaust, O2 monitors
recommended_check_or_change: Duct the relief outlet and pump exhaust out of the VLM; an automatic shut-off on the argon at the dock when the tray is stowed or the machine idle; low-level O2 monitors inside the VLM bay and at the opening; check the worst case (one cylinder into the VLM volume)
evidence: secondary summary of a CSB report + national-lab guidance

pain_point: Enclosed VLM towers hide fires and defeat sprinklers
what_happened: Kardex with Fike: VLM towers reach 30 ft or more; the enclosure limits airflow, so heat and smoke build undetected; sprinklers are designed for open shelving; they recommend aspirating smoke detection and an IG-100 (nitrogen) clean-agent system
root_cause: Enclosed, dense storage; suppression designed for other hazards
implication_for_this_design: An Al powder or condensate fire inside a VLM meets either water (reacts with Al) or nitrogen (Mg burns in N2, the reason for the lab's argon rule); Powderpart was cited partly because sprinklers could not be disconnected
design_element: VLM integration (byu-vcl PR 318), dust hazard analysis
recommended_check_or_change: Ask EHS and the VLM vendor what suppression the unit has; limit powder on the tray to one reservoir plus the overflow; put a smoke or heat sensor inside the guard that stops the machine and alarms; include the VLM in the DHA

pain_point: The VLM moves a tray with a build in progress
what_happened: Our own transit check (low-profile.md §4.2) assumed 2 m/s² horizontal and ±3 m/s² vertical tray motion; the dock (mains, argon, Ethernet) mates sideways and parts when the tray leaves
root_cause: No interlock between the VLM controller and the machine's state
implication_for_this_design: A tray called mid-build would shake a loose powder bed and full reservoir, cut services under a hot plate, and move a machine whose laser may be enabled
design_element: VLM interface, tray dock, UPS, supervisor
recommended_check_or_change: Make the tray un-callable while lasing, off atmosphere, hot or mid-build (a hardware permissive to the VLM, not just software); define a safe pause (shutter closed, heaters to a hold, valves closed) for a forced recall; test it
evidence: derived from this repo (no external incident)

pain_point: Factory-built interlocks can be wrong
what_happened: FDA Class 2 recall (initiated 8 Aug 2024): Epilog Fusion Pro 24, Model 17000, 751 units in commerce; 'a small number ... were released with an incorrectly placed Interlock device', so the laser could run with the front door open; fixed by a repair kit
root_cause: Assembly error in a safety interlock, not caught by final test
implication_for_this_design: Our guard door, panels, drawer and service covers all carry interlocks built in-house; the engraver route (README §1b.1) starts from a bought machine whose interlocks are then modified
design_element: guard interlocks, safety relay
recommended_check_or_change: Proof-test every interlock at commissioning and after any panel change: open each door or panel with emission requested into a dump and confirm the shutter and laser drop; record it in a checklist the LSO signs

pain_point: 2 m/s cross-flow is the threshold, not a margin, and small chambers recirculate
what_happened: Reijonen et al. 2020: porosity stayed < 0.1 % at 2.5-4.0 m/s but rose sharply at <= 2.0 m/s, with unstable melt pools and balling; Shen et al. 2020: ~4 m/s at the inlet decayed to ~1 m/s at the outlet in a commercial machine, and too much flow picks up powder; Griggs et al. 2021 (MIT compact testbed): baffles and guide vanes only moved recirculation, a second upper nozzle suppressed it at the window; Medinilla et al. 2025: an EOS M290 recirculation zone was removed by eliminating a backward-facing step; Kjer et al. 2023 (DTU): low-velocity regions matched porosity (all via Edison)
root_cause: Velocity decays across the plate; a short, small chamber recirculates plume and soot
implication_for_this_design: README §3.4 designs for ~2 m/s at the plate through a 120 x 8 mm slot (~115 L/min); the chamber is 120 mm tall with the outlet in the floor; the window gas knife is in effect Griggs' secondary nozzle (good)
design_element: cross-flow inlet and outlet, blower, window gas knife
recommended_check_or_change: Size the blower for >= 2.5 m/s measured over the whole usable plate with headroom to ~4 m/s (about 145-230 L/min through the 120 x 8 mm slot, calc); find each powder's pick-up limit; map velocity on a grid with a hot-wire or Pitot plus smoke before first builds; keep the knife's flow separately adjustable; check for steps between inlet, floor and plate

pain_point: 200 °C preheat does not stop cracking in crack-prone wrought alloys
what_happened: Velikajne et al. 2026: EN AW-7075 preheated to 100-200 °C showed no significant drop in crack density, and 400 °C gave columnar crack networks and lower hardness; Riener et al. 2022: Zr-modified 6182 was crack-free and > 99.0 % dense only at 500 °C (via Edison)
root_cause: Hot cracking follows freezing range and grain structure; moderate preheat does not change them
implication_for_this_design: Tier A plates run at 200 °C; 500 °C is reserved (Tier B, preheat-and-plates.md); screening unrefined 2xxx/6xxx/7xxx at 200 °C will mostly measure cracking
design_element: heated build module tiers, alloy campaign plan
recommended_check_or_change: Scope the first screening campaigns to AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr and grain-refined alloys; run crack-prone wrought alloys only as Tier B (steel or ceramic block, 500 °C) campaigns; include a known crack-prone control coupon

pain_point: Edge effects shrink the usable area of small plates
what_happened: Jacob et al. 2016 (NIST): wall effects on powder packing grow as the layer thickness approaches particle size; the Edison review's engineering estimate is that a Ø25 plate keeps ~17-21 mm usable (46-71 % of its area) and a Ø75 plate ~67-71 mm (80-90 %)
root_cause: Wall packing, recoater overshoot, the rim gap and flow boundary effects at the cylinder edge
implication_for_this_design: Our S25 module is the alloy-saving option; coupons near its rim wiper see different packing and gas flow
design_element: coupon layout on S25/M50/L75
recommended_check_or_change: Keep coupons >= 2-3 mm inside the rim; on the first builds put witness coupons at the edge and centre and compare density; record each coupon's radial position in the dataset

pain_point: Seal drag can pull the piston off its magnetic coupling
what_happened: The Edison design review flags seal drag, stick-slip and magnetic-coupling slip as Z errors to qualify under load at temperature (a research testbed's 5 µm increments are not accuracy; Oropeza et al. 2021). Our own numbers: hot-swap.md puts the M50 break-out drag at ~133 N (two FKM rod O-rings 87 N plus the bore seal), and the pot magnet that pulls the piston down breaks away at ~217 N with clean faces but keeps only ~27 % of its force across a 0.1 mm gap
root_cause: A friction load close to a magnet's pull; one powder grain on the striker removes the margin
implication_for_this_design: With a grain on the striker the magnet holds ~59 N, under the ~133 N drag (calc): the arm moves down, the piston stays, the next layer is ~0 µm thick and the blade hits the part
design_element: Z coupling (pot magnet), bore seal, rod gland
recommended_check_or_change: Measure the piston's actual position (a displacement sensor between arm and rod end, or an encoder on the rod) and fault on a missed step; test magnet pull against seal break-out at 200 °C with powder present; replace the magnet with a positive coupling (the planned drawbar or ball lock)
evidence: derived from this repo's calcs + Edison review

pain_point: Closed or analog controls obsolete or degrade a machine
what_happened: Aagaard et al. 2023 (DTU, via Edison): a Realizer 250 became inoperable when its DOS control PC crashed: no service agreement, black-box electronics, mechanically sound otherwise (mean LPBF price ~EUR 410k in 2022); Andersen et al. 2022: DTU's first-generation analog scanner interfaces picked up electrical noise, so the second generation went fully digital (XY2-100) and separated hard-real-time laser control
root_cause: Closed controllers without source or service; analog command lines in a noisy cabinet
implication_for_this_design: The engraver route may start from a locked EZCAD/JCZ board (Windows-only, README §1b.1); the IPG laser takes analog 0-10 V power; the supervisor is a Pi
design_element: scan and laser controller, analog power line, software repository
recommended_check_or_change: Keep all control code and configuration in git with a spare controller board; prefer open protocols (XY2-100, DTU controller, an SDK); run the analog power line as short shielded twisted pair grounded at the laser and check power ripple with the photodiode at fixed set points

pain_point: Monitoring data mislead unless tied to machine state, and slow displays cannot stop a crash
what_happened: Maddison 2022 (thesis, Aconity MINI, via Edison): the pyrometer kept logging during laser-off travel and pauses, giving false low readings and dark lines in thermal maps; Friedo et al. 2026: an MPrint+'s free software refreshed live monitoring only every few seconds, too slow to intervene in recoater failures, and dust and vapour added sensor noise; Calta et al. 2018 (LLNL): laser trigger timing had to be corrected empirically for galvo acceleration
root_cause: Sensor streams not synchronised with the laser gate and galvo position; people in the loop are slow
implication_for_this_design: Our photodiode check (low-profile.md §4.5), layer-camera scoring and the screening dataset all depend on clean, time-aligned signals; the machine is meant to run with a robot and nobody watching
design_element: supervisor logging, scan controller, photodiode, layer camera
recommended_check_or_change: Sample the photodiode on the scan controller's clock with the laser gate and galvo position and mask laser-off data; tune laser on/off delays and skywriting on a test pattern; make aborts automatic in the supervisor (torque spike, coverage, O2, dew point) rather than relying on someone watching a stream
evidence: papers and thesis via Edison (DOIs where given)
